newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Liberals to split any budget surplus.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Liberals to split any budget surplus.

text.p: Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberals promised on Wednesday they would spend half of any budget surplus on new programs and allocate the rest to debt reduction and debt relief if they were re-elected on June 2.

A copy of their new campaign platform, nicknamed Red Book Two, was distributed to reporters on Wednesday afternoon, a day after Reform Party leader Preston Manning scooped the Liberals by releasing selected details contained in it.
It said Canada was moving towards the time when the budget would finally be balanced and the government would have a surplus.

"When we reach that time, we will allocate every billion dollars of fiscal dividend so that one half will go to a combination of reducing taxes and reducing the national debt, and one half will address social and economic needs through program expenditures," the document pledged.

The document listed C$6.50 billion in new spending planned over the coming years, starting with C$43 million in 1997-98, C$1.06 billion in 1998-99, C$1.83 billion each of the next two years, and C$1.73 billion for 2001-02.
Of this, C$4.80 billion had been announced on Monday in the form of reversing planned health and social transfer cuts.

Besides those transfer payments, it planned C$615.8 million over the five years in other health spending to deal with problems ranging from AIDS and breast cancer to aboriginal health and and tobacco.

An additional C$240 million would go to grants for students with dependents, C$216 million on youth, C$182 million on economic development and C$443.6 million on programs ranging from crime prevention to the arts.
Besides this C$6.50 billion in spending, the Liberals also said they intended to at least double the C$850 million increase they have made to the new Canada Child Tax Benefit.
This increased child benefit would be done "as resources become available."

In terms of pharmacare, or national drug insurance, it said that as soon as a plan and timetable had been devised and enough provinces came on board, the Liberals would "make a significant contribution to bringing it to reality."
It did not mention how much this would add to spending, but the Reform Party charged it could be as much as C$3.5 billion.
Regarding taxes, it said: "To propose a broad-based tax cut at this time is to pretend that the attack on the deficit is over, when it is not.
It said any broad-based tax cut today would be unacceptable since this would have to be paid for by adding to the deficit or by cutting government programs further.

"Targeted tax cuts have been implemented already, and more selective tax cuts will be made. The time for a broad-based tax reduction will come, when we can afford it as a society and when Canadians can be assured that such cuts can be permanent," it said.

It said the Liberals would not spend any of the contingency reserves on new programs or tax cuts, and said the C$6.5 billion in new spending would be funded by exceeding the deficit target by more than the contingency reserve or by reallocations within the fiscal framework if necessary.
The document indicated the deficit for 1996-97 would be less than C$16 billion, compared with the original C$24.3 billion and the "no more than C$19 billion" mentioned in February.

It did not specifically mention C$16 billion, a figure Finance Minister Paul Martin said this week would not be unreasonable, but said the government had sought to reduce the deficit from C$42 billion when they took office and added: "Indeed, the deficit for 1996-97 will be well below our target and more than C$26 billion lower than it was when we took office."
The Liberals said they were giving their highest priority to keeping francophone Quebec in Canada.
"Keeping Canada united is our single most important commitment. The government of Canada can have no greater duty or responsibility," the new Red Book said.

It repeated the Liberal view that the distinctiveness of Quebec must be enshrined in the constitution, a position that has not satisfied hard-line separatists and has angered some in the rest of Canada, particularly in the Reform Party.
"Our platform outlines a balanced set of priorities for the future," Chretien said in a statement.

"It's a balanced, practical plan. We'll build on our record by maintaining our commitment to fiscal responsibility, and making the investments required to strengthen our economy and take Canada into the 21st century."
((Randall Palmer, Reuters Ottawa Bureau 613-235-6745))
